concept: Automated concentrated-liquidity range management bots on Base

claims.text: Base documents the GasPriceOracle getL1Fee method for a serialized transaction and getL1FeeUpperBound for an approximate byte length. These provide transaction-size-sensitive estimates of the L1 component. (low confidence)

For Base transaction-cost scenarios, the network-fee documentation gives total cost as execution gas times base plus priority fee, plus L1 fee and operator fee. Subtracting only the execution component would omit costs named by the documentation. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05)

Make repeated triggers harmless: Chainlink says completed work must change state so the same subset is no longer eligible, and AWS recommends caller-provided request identifiers for recognizing duplicate requests. Inference for an LP bot: give each intended action a durable identity and reconcile its outcome before issuing another action for the same intent; an offchain identifier alone does not enforce onchain idempotency. (medium confidence)

Persist operation identity and request parameters together when implementing an idempotent control API: AWS describes atomic recording of the token and mutations, and rejecting reused identifiers when parameters change. This is evidence for durable intent records, not a claim that a local database commit can atomically commit a blockchain transaction. (low confidence)

Negation finding: the optimal-range paper assumes flat, constant gas fees and continuously adjusted positions; it says continuous trading requires large initial wealth to overcome gas fees. Its proposed discrete alternative is to adjust when drift or fee profitability changes substantially, so its analytic optimum is not a ready-made rebalance cadence for a small bot. (low confidence)

Revert Auto-Range documents a percentage-out-of-range trigger followed by withdrawal and recreation at the same width centered on current price. Its fee-source documentation also says inadequate gas budget can prevent triggering; the feature description is not a guarantee of uninterrupted range activity. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05)

Krystal documents independent lower/upper trigger prices, a time buffer requiring price to remain outside the trigger band, and a separately configured destination range. Its gas-fee ceiling can defer a rebalance. These controls illustrate that the trigger band, dwell time and new range are separate choices. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05)

Steer documents distinct trigger families: distance from range center, inactive range, percentage drift relative to range, directional range exit, and no automatic price trigger. It explicitly cautions that more frequent rebalancing raises gas costs and that triggers should reflect expected pair volatility. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05)

Base documents ETH as the currency of its Mainnet and lists separate public RPC and transaction-submission endpoints for Mainnet and Sepolia. It says to use the transaction submission endpoint only to send transactions and the RPC endpoint for all other requests; use these network settings when configuring an Ethereum wallet library for Base. (low confidence)

Viem createNonceManager automatically generates transaction nonces for Local Accounts. The documentation assigns nonce management for JSON-RPC Accounts to their wallet or backend; it does not describe this manager as a cross-process coordinator. (low confidence)

Base fee budgeting must account for L1 publication cost as well as L2 execution. Its detailed fee formula also includes operatorFee; the documentation says getOperatorFee returns zero when operator-fee parameters are zero. Do not treat gasUsed times effectiveGasPrice alone as the full fee. (low confidence)

Safe implements ERC-4337 compatibility through Safe4337Module and a fallback handler. Its documented flow validates owner signatures on a UserOperation and executes it through EntryPoint; this flow does not itself establish a separate bot session-key permission policy. (low confidence)

EIP-7702 sets persistent EOA code delegation. A processed delegation is not rolled back when transaction execution fails; the viem guide likewise shows subsequent calls without a new authorization. (medium confidence)

Viem documents executor: self for signAuthorization when the authorizing EOA also executes the transaction, because authorization.nonce must be one greater than transaction.nonce. The EIP processes authorization tuples after incrementing the sender nonce. (medium confidence)
For fee estimation, distinguish active liquidity from total deposited capital: a position stops earning swap fees when price leaves its interval. (medium confidence)

The Uniswap math primer derives current position holdings from liquidity, lower and upper ticks, and the pool square-root price. Use its separate in-range and out-of-range formulas when marking a simulated position to market. (low confidence)

Krystal documents a Gas Fee Ceiling: if the estimated rebalance cost exceeds the ceiling, Auto-Rebalance does not trigger. This provides a concrete execution-cost gate alongside its slippage controls. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05)

Revert documents sourcing auto-range swaps through the 0x aggregator and applying the configured maximum price impact as the swap execution threshold. This is evidence of an aggregator-based rebalance implementation, not a verified claim that its quoted price is globally optimal. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05)

A timeout is an ambiguous outcome, not evidence of absence of side effects. AWS recommends connection and request timeouts, capped backoff, a limit on retry attempts, a single retry layer where practical, and jitter; apply these controls to bot RPC dependencies and reconcile state-changing operations before retrying them. (low confidence)

Gamma attributed its January 2024 vault exploit to an arithmetic error in automation scripts that configured deposit safety settings, and reported that halting deposits stopped the attack vector while withdrawals remained possible; the operational lesson inferred here is to validate applied risk configuration and rehearse selective emergency controls. (low confidence)

Fees alone do not establish LP profitability. The LVR paper separates market-risk exposure from a microstructural component of fees minus arbitrage losses, while the optimal-range paper balances fees against predictable loss, concentration risk and rebalancing costs. (medium confidence)

Charm describes a multi-position Alpha Vault strategy: full-range liquidity, a concentrated base order and a limit order. Managers choose concentration and out-of-range depth through parameters; this is a different strategy family from repeatedly moving one fixed-width band. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05)

In its continuous-time model, the LVR paper decomposes LP returns into market-risk exposure and a microstructure component consisting of accrued fees minus losses to arbitrageurs; fee revenue alone therefore does not describe LP returns. (low confidence)

Architecture recommendation inferred from the documented check/perform pattern: separate observation and planning from state-changing execution; the execution boundary must recheck current conditions rather than trust an earlier plan. Chainlink documents offchain checks and onchain performance as one example of this separation, without establishing present service availability. (low confidence)

Base derivation distinguishes unsafe, safe, and finalized chain state and can reorganize above the safe block. Architectural inference: store block identity with observations, treat provisional observations as revisable, and replay/reconcile affected bot records after a reorganization instead of declaring every observed inclusion permanent. (low confidence)

Google recommends monitoring latency, traffic, errors, and saturation and keeping paging noise low. Inference for an LP bot: instrument dependency latency and errors, job throughput and backlog, and alert on actionable loss of progress rather than paging on every transient retry. (low confidence)

Narrower ranges concentrate fee earning while active but increase concentration risk and exposure to volatility-related loss. Cartea, Drissi and Monga derive an incentive to widen ranges as volatility increases; Gamma also describes narrow positions as more short volatility. This is a conditional tradeoff, not a universal optimal width. (medium confidence)

In the Cartea–Drissi–Monga model, optimal range width depends on fees after gas, predictable loss and concentration risk. The strategy optimizes expected utility of terminal wealth rather than fee income alone. (low confidence)

The optimal-control paper allows a predictive drift signal to skew the range rather than always centering it symmetrically. That result is model-dependent and requires a signal; it does not establish a profitable directional forecast for Base pools. (low confidence)

Impermanent loss and loss-versus-rebalancing compare against different benchmarks: holding the initial assets versus an idealized portfolio that follows AMM holdings through frictionless external trading. The term rebalancing in LVR does not mean a bot moving a concentrated-liquidity range. (low confidence)

ERC-7715 defines wallet_requestExecutionPermissions with a chainId, session account in to, permission and optional rules; the returned response may differ from the request. Discover supported permission and rule types rather than assuming every wallet accepts the same policy. (low confidence)

ERC-7715 defines permission revocation and retrieval methods and says unsupported wallets should return an error. Its interface specifies wallet-to-DApp interaction rather than how the wallet enforces permissions. (low confidence)

The open-source Uniswap v3 Active Strategy Framework uses historical swap data for simulations and describes block-level virtual liquidity as an input for approximating fee income. It is a reference implementation, rather than evidence that an arbitrary target pool has been backtested correctly. (low confidence)

The framework explicitly warns that it omits gas costs and may suffer Python-versus-Solidity rounding differences and a price feed that differs from the pool price. Treat its simulated results as estimates until these limitations are addressed. (low confidence)

Aero documentation distinguishes staked LP positions earning AERO rewards from unstaked LP positions retaining Smart Fees minus an unstaked fee; Smart Fees from the staked positions go to Token Operators. A backtest should model the selected mode rather than crediting both revenue streams to the same position. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05)

Uniswap’s routeToRatio configuration separates ratioErrorTolerance from maxIterations; the former bounds ratio error and the latter limits the search, returning an error if the iteration limit is exceeded. These are ratio-search controls, rather than substitutes for swap slippage limits. (low confidence)

Uniswap’s v3 Quoter relies on state-changing calls that revert to return quote data; the guide recommends offchain simulation via callStatic rather than an expensive onchain Quoter call. Its quoteExactInputSingle example returns the quoted output amount. (low confidence)

Aero describes an MEV-tax module that increases the pool’s extra swap fee when the transaction priority fee exceeds a threshold. The same source says deployment will be gradual; applicability to a particular pool must be checked rather than assumed. Consequently, raising a priority fee can affect swap economics where that module is active. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05)

Bound each automated work item: Chainlink recommends limiting check and execution ranges and splitting work across registrations to keep execution inside predictable gas limits. For an LP controller, bounding the number of positions handled per job is an application of that pattern. (low confidence)

OpenZeppelin documents an authorized emergency stop, but inheriting the pause module does not automatically protect every function: the relevant function modifiers must actually be applied. A bot-owned executor needs explicit coverage of the critical entry points it intends to stop. (low confidence)

Do not assume a dependency circuit breaker is automatically the best retry control: AWS warns that circuit breakers introduce modal behavior that is difficult to test and can delay recovery, and describes local token-bucket retry limits as an alternative. This caution concerns dependency overload handling, not a reason to omit an emergency stop for bot-controlled financial operations. (low confidence)

Concentrated liquidity allocates capital to a chosen price interval. A position stops earning trading fees outside that interval; leaving the interval is an earning-state change, not itself an instruction to rebalance. (medium confidence)

An out-of-range position can become active again without recentering if price returns. Uniswap describes the position becoming entirely one asset at the boundary; a bot must treat waiting and changing its range as distinct strategy choices. (low confidence)

Negation finding: Willetts and Harrington argue that frictionless LVR is an imperfect measure for comparing execution venues and propose RVR with centralized rebalancing frictions. Their paper focuses on fixed-weight and dynamic-weight AMMs, so it does not demonstrate that a Slipstream range-recentering bot is profitable. (low confidence)

Aero describes Slipstream rewards as restricted to liquidity in the active range and says out-of-range single-sided deposits can express a directional range-order view. Strategy design must distinguish active earning from intentionally resting outside the market. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05)

Arrakis Pro describes treasury-owned liquidity for token issuers. Its Flagship strategy concentrates around spot and adapts to volatility; its market-making system monitors price, volatility and inventory to choose rebalances. These are issuer inventory objectives, which should not be assumed identical to a personal LP bot objective. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05)

In its historical Arbitrum launch description, Gamma distinguishes market-price reset bounds for dynamic wide/narrow ranges from NAV-based reset bounds for pegged-price assets. The latter may deliberately remain out of range while market price deviates from NAV; this is historical strategy evidence, not verification of present Base or Slipstream support. (low confidence)

Viem Local Accounts keep signing keys on the consuming machine and sign before JSON-RPC broadcast. Its documented setup creates a Wallet Client and constructs a local account with privateKeyToAccount. (low confidence)

The viem local-account example extends a Wallet Client with publicActions and calls a contract simulation public action before a contract write wallet action; these are separate public simulation and wallet write actions. (low confidence)

web3.py documents explicit offline signing with sign_transaction followed by send_raw_transaction, or automatic signing through SignAndSendRawMiddlewareBuilder. Its guide says never to commit the private key in code. (low confidence)

The web3.py explicit transaction example obtains nonce from get_transaction_count and sets gas, maxFeePerGas, and maxPriorityFeePerGas before signing; contract calls can use build_transaction before the same signing and submission stages. (low confidence)

Safe Modules can automate DeFi actions without manual approvals, but enabled modules validate requests using their own rules and can execute arbitrary transactions. Safe explicitly warns that a malicious module can take over a Safe. (low confidence)

EIP-7702 enables weaker sub-key permissions as a design goal, but secure delegate code must enforce replay protection and bind value, gas, target and calldata. ERC-7715 separately says wallet implementations must correctly enforce granted permissions and recommends limited scope and reasonable expiry. (medium confidence)

The cached ERC-7715 source is marked Draft. Treat the described method names as a proposal interface and verify the selected wallet implementation before depending on it. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05)

For a fixed-liquidity accounting interval, the Uniswap primer calculates uncollected token fees as position liquidity times the change in inside-range fee growth, divided by the fixed-point scaling factor; pool and tick inputs must refer to the same block. (low confidence)

The RVR authors distinguish impermanent loss, which uses a holding benchmark, from LVR and RVR, which evaluate rebalancing. They caution that efficiently executing a poor asset-management strategy does not make it a good strategy. Report these benchmark comparisons separately. (low confidence)

The RVR paper scopes its critique of LVR to benchmark realism: the idealized centralized exchange has no fees, spread, or slippage. This does not establish that a concentrated-liquidity bot on Base will outperform holding. (low confidence)

A rebalance swap must target the token ratio required by the new liquidity position, and the swap itself can change that ratio. Uniswap documents atomic swap-and-add execution; Revert cautions that aggregator execution and concurrent swaps can still leave tokens after minting, which its implementation returns to the owner. Atomic execution should not be interpreted as a guarantee of zero dust. (medium confidence)

Uniswap’s swap-and-add guide configures the leftover-dust recipient, slippageTolerance and deadline in swap options, and uses tokenId to identify the existing position. Treat this as a documented Uniswap integration pattern; direct compatibility with Aero routers is not established here. (low confidence)

Uniswap documents quoteExactInputSingle and quoteExactOutputSingle for one pool, and quoteExactInput and quoteExactOutput for multiple pools. Exact-input quotes solve for output; exact-output quotes solve for required input. (low confidence)

Execution safeguards need to cover both swapping and liquidity placement: Krystal exposes separate Pool Slippage and Swap Slippage controls that can revert a transaction; Revert describes a maximum-price-impact threshold including pool fee, price impact and possible slippage, plus a pool-TWAP cross-check against price manipulation. These vendor mechanisms have different semantics and should not be treated as interchangeable settings. (medium confidence)

Flashbots Protect’s overview describes protection for transactions on Ethereum and submission through rpc.flashbots.net/fast. That page alone does not establish a Base-compatible private submission route, so an LP bot should not infer Base support from the Flashbots name. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05)

Base’s documentation gives conflicting deployment status: the Flashblocks reference calls Denim deprecation planned and not finalized, while the November 5, 2026 Base Engineering announcement says Denim is live and Flashblocks streams and pending preconfirmation state are retired. Preserve this as an attributed status conflict; confirm the target RPC’s deployed behavior before choosing Flashblocks-specific quoting or subscription semantics. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05)

Private-mempool sandwich findings depend on the measurement scope. How to Serve Your Sandwich reports strong execution constraints and limits its analysis to same-block patterns, acknowledging possible cross-block attacks. No Place to Hide reports Base attacks associated with an RPC leak and predictable victim behavior, including wider and cross-block patterns. These attributed results do not justify a blanket guarantee that Base private submission prevents sandwiching. (low confidence)

Base’s Denim announcement distinguishes fast inclusion from finality: a block becomes safe after its batch is posted to Ethereum and final after Ethereum finalizes that batch. A fast receipt alone therefore does not establish final settlement of a rebalance. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05)
